problem: The x-axis runs linearly from 1 to 10¹² while the plotted quantity is 10 log₁₀(I/I₀). On a linear axis almost the whole curve is squashed against the y-axis, so the reader cannot see that each tenfold rise adds 10 dB, which is exactly the point the figure caption makes.
fix: Use a logarithmic x-axis for I/I₀ (1, 10, 10², … 10¹²); the plotted line then becomes a straight line of slope 10 dB per decade.

problem: The sample points jump straight from x = 1 to x ≈ 1.25×10¹⁰. Joined as a polyline on the linear axis, the first segment is a straight chord from 0 dB to about 101 dB, so the drawn curve is not the logarithm over that whole first stretch.
fix: Add sample points at 10, 10², 10³ … so the drawn segments follow 10 log₁₀(I/I₀) closely, or plot on a log x-axis where the curve is a straight line.

problem: 'measured in m² sabins' uses two unit names for the same thing; the sabin is already defined as equivalent to 1 m² of perfect absorption, so a student may think absorption has a unit different from area.
fix: Write 'A = Σ αᵢ Sᵢ, in square metres (the unit is also called the sabin)'.

problem: The trap warns against I₀ = 10⁻⁶ W/m², a value students rarely meet. The confusion that actually happens is between 10⁻¹² W/m² and the older 10⁻¹⁶ W/cm² form.
fix: Say: do not use I₀ = 10⁻¹⁶ W/cm² (an old cgs form); in SI the air reference is 10⁻¹² W/m², which equals 10⁻¹⁶ W/cm².
